about: The words of the lender's stick (Data/encounters/wokerer_793.json): the Wōkerer's man, the day, the clean stick. Placeholders for the user's own. The man's name is the user's to give.

entries.text: The Wōkerer's man
God keep you. It is Bubo again.
You said next time. I think this is next time.
I have thought about that bread of yours since.
You told me the purse was empty, and then I saw that it was not. I did not tell him. I would rather not have to.
Your men said you were ashore. I saw your feet under the sail. It is no matter.
It is close to Michaelmas now. He has started to count the days at table, between dishes.
Is there anything for the stick today? Any sum will do. I have the knife with me.
Count him out a pound (240 d)

He counts it twice, slowly, moving his lips. Then he lays the two halves of the stick together on his knee and cuts one notch clean off both. He shows you the stick afterwards, as if you might not believe him.
Count him out sixty pennies

He counts it into a cloth and ties the cloth. Sixty pennies is a quarter of a notch, so he scores the next notch across with the point of his knife, once. He says it all goes on, and that the Wōkerer looks.
Pay him all that is on the stick

It takes him a long time to count, and he does it twice. Then he cuts every notch off both halves, blows the chips away, and looks at the bare stick for a while. He says he has never carried one home clean. He says the Wōkerer will want to see you himself, and will not say why.
Sit him down and feed him (2 d)

He eats like a man who has been thinking about it for some days. He praises the bread, then the cheese, then the bread again. Then he wipes his knife and asks, kindly, whether there was anything for the stick. There was not. He thanks you all the same, and says he will come by.
Not today. Tell him next time
He nods. He writes nothing down, because he cannot write. He does not seem put out. He asks where you are bound next, and you find you have told him.
Tell him the purse is empty
He looks at your face, and then at his shoes. Then there is nothing to cut, he says, and he will tell the Wōkerer so. He believes you. You had not thought that would be the worse of the two.
He says nothing. He looks at the purse on your belt until you look at it too. He says he will tell the Wōkerer there was nothing today. He says that part is true.
Get under the sail and have the men say you are ashore

He stands by the boat for a long while, eating. The men tell him you are up at the market. He thanks them, and says he will wait, and then that he will not, and goes. Brunger laughs until he has to sit down.

The men say you are ashore, and none of them says it well. Bubo looks at the sail, which has your foot under it, and says he is sorry to have missed you. Nobody laughs this time. Aldger does not look at you until evening.
A man sits on the dam head by your berth with a split hazel stick across his knees and half a loaf in his lap. He stands up when you step ashore, and brushes off the crumbs first.

God keep you. I am Bubo. I carry the other half of your stick for the Wōkerer, and I am to ask you, wherever I find you, whether there is anything to cut off it today. Any sum will do. I have the knife with me.

God keep you. I am Bubo. I carry the other half of your stick for the Wōkerer, and I am to ask you, wherever I find you, whether there is anything to cut off it today. I did not think it would be so far.
I was sick from the river mouth to here. I do not think the sea is meant for a man who likes his dinner.
They will not take the king's pennies here, so I have eaten what I brought. It was not enough.

At first light there is a man on the jetty who was not there last night. He sits on a post with a hazel stick across his knees, peeling a boiled egg. He is a bad colour. He came in on another ship, he says, and he does not say which.
Alongside, in the fog
Fog. A boat is alongside before the lookout has finished saying so. In her bow a man holds a hazel stick in one hand and her gunwale in the other. He is the colour of the fog.
God keep you. It is Bubo. I will not come aboard, I thank you. If I let go of this I shall be ill. Is there anything for the stick? I can take it over the side.
Hand him the bread bag across
Tell him this is no place for it

He lets go of the gunwale to take it, which is brave of him. He says God reward you, and then he cannot say anything for a while. His boat falls astern into the fog. You can hear him thanking you after you can no longer see him.
He says he sees that, and that he said as much to the man who rowed him. He lifts the stick to you as his boat falls astern, the way another man would lift his cap.
Two men and a rope
Count out all of it
Tell him you have not got it
The Wōkerer is on the dam head himself, on a stool he has had carried down, with a dish on his knee. Two men stand behind him with a coil of rope. Bubo stands behind them, looking at his shoes.
Michaelmas. I said the day, and I said I would not stay to hear why. Count it out.
The day is past. I was here on the day. You were not. Count it out.
I told him you would come.
He counts it himself. He does not weigh it. It takes as long as his dish does. Then he nods to the two men, and they carry their rope back up the bank without a word. One of them looks sorry to go.

He does not look up, and he does not ask what is in your purse. Then she works for him, he says, until the stick is clean. You are to sail her as you did. Half of what she sells comes to him before it comes to you, and Bubo goes with you and counts it. One of the two men ties the rope to your stem post, looks at him, and unties it again. That was all the rope was for.
Bubo is on the jetty, and for once he is not eating. Two men stand behind him with a coil of rope. They came in on another ship. All three of them have been sick.
God keep you. The day is past, and he sent the rope with us. I am sorry for it. If you have all of it, I am to take it. If you have not, I am to say what he said, word for word.

He counts it twice on the planks, with the two men holding the corners of the cloth down against the wind. Then he cuts the stick clean. He says the Wōkerer will want to see you at home, and not to ask him why: he has never brought one back clean. The two men carry their rope aboard the next ship south.

He shuts his eyes and says it as it was said to him. She works for the Wōkerer until the stick is clean. You are to sail her as you did. Half of what she sells goes to him before it comes to you, and Bubo counts it. He opens his eyes. That is all of it, he says. He is to sail with you now. He is sorry for that too. He is not a good sailor.
A clean stick
Take your half of the stick
Leave both halves on his table
The Wōkerer is at his table. Both halves of your stick lie beside his dish, with no notch left on either. He is looking at them, and not at you.
It is clean. Most are not.
She is yours. You owe me nothing and I owe you nothing. Shut the door behind you.
She's ours! Yours, I mean. I come with her, that's all I meant.

He pushes one half across the table with the back of his knife and goes on eating. It is lighter than you thought it would be. Outside, Ravn asks to hold it, and then cannot think what to do with it, and gives it back.
You leave them where they lie. At the door you look back. He has put both halves on the fire under his pot, and is watching to see that they catch.
The Wōkerer is at his table. Both halves of your stick lie beside his dish, with no notch left on either. Bubo stands by the door with his cap in his hands.
It is clean. It was late, and it is clean. She is yours again. Bubo comes ashore.
I shall miss the bread. I shall not miss the sea.

He pushes one half across the table with the back of his knife. Bubo walks you down to the boat and stands on the dam head until you have let go. He lifts his cap. He is, for the first time since you have known him, a good colour.
You leave them where they lie. Behind you, you hear him tell Bubo to put them on the fire, and Bubo ask whether he might keep one.
The counter aboard
Bubo sits against the mast with the stick in his lap and his eyes shut. He has not eaten since the river mouth. Every time she rolls he says a saint's name, and he is running out of saints.
I am to count what she sells. He did not say I had to look at the water. I would be glad not to.
He is sitting on the halyard. Either he moves or the yard stays where it is.
Put him in the bow, out of the way, with a hide over him
Give him an oar. Work is the cure
Brunger lifts him like a sack and sets him down in the bow under a hide. He thanks everybody by name. An hour later he asks, from under the hide, whether anything has been sold yet.
He rows for the length of a psalm, badly, and is sick over the oar, and goes on rowing. The men stop laughing somewhere in the second hour. By evening they are calling the stroke for him.

Morning on a timber dam head: a plump, mild man in a plain brown cloak sits beside a small open boat with a split hazel stick across his knees and half a loaf in his lap; he is half risen, brushing crumbs from his front.

First light on a strange jetty, mist on the water: the same mild man sits on a mooring post peeling an egg, a hazel stick across his knees, pale and a little green; behind him a foreign ship he has plainly just left.
Thick fog at sea: a rowing boat close alongside the small open boat, and in her bow the mild man holding a hazel stick in one hand and the gunwale in the other, his eyes shut.

A grey Michaelmas on the dam head: a lean grey man sits on a stool eating from a dish on his knee and does not look up; two men stand behind him with a coil of rope; behind them the mild man looks at his shoes.
A far jetty in wind: the mild man stands with his cap off and nothing in his hands; two men behind him hold a coil of rope; all three are pale.
Inside a plain timber house by lamplight: the lean grey man at a table with a dish before him; beside the dish lie two halves of a hazel stick with no notch on either; he looks at the stick.
The same table and the same two halves of a bare hazel stick; the mild man stands by the door with his cap in his hands.
At sea in a small open boat under sail: the mild man sits against the mast with a hazel stick in his lap and his eyes shut, pale; the steersman points past him at a rope.
you told the lender's man the purse was empty, and he saw that it was not
the men saw you hide under the sail
